title: Huge Study Links Screen Time to Developmental Issues
paragraphs: Many parents worry about how much time their children spend looking at screens. Now, a huge new study has found that more screen time is linked to poorer development in children, although the effects appear to be relatively small.

The study was led by Sheri Madigan, a professor of psychology at the University of Calgary in Canada, and it was published in the journal JAMA Pediatrics in September 2026. The researchers combined the results of decades of earlier research, covering nearly three million children aged 18 and under in 64 countries.

The researchers found that greater screen time was linked to poorer outcomes in several areas of development, including thinking, learning, speech, behavior and the ability to control emotions. Interestingly, newer studies showed stronger links than older ones. Madigan suggested that this may be because today's devices are portable, interactive and responsive, unlike the televisions of the past.
However, most of the links were relatively small. Nevertheless, Madigan argued that even small effects matter, because screen use is now so common among children.

Other experts praised the research. Esther van Sluijs, a professor at Loughborough University in the UK who was not involved in the study, described it as high-quality. Tatiana Íñiguez Berrozpe of the University of Zaragoza in Spain called it methodologically very sound, although she pointed out that the link with mental health and school performance was very small.

It is important to note that the study only shows a link between screen time and development. It does not prove that screens cause these problems. For example, children who are already struggling may turn to screens more often. In addition, according to van Sluijs, there was not enough data to draw conclusions about specific activities, such as social media or gaming.

Madigan does not believe parents should see screens as bad in themselves. Instead, she advises them to think about how devices are used, and to notice when screens take time away from sleep, physical activity, play, learning or spending time with other people. Simple steps, such as having dinners without devices or choosing a daily time when the whole family puts their devices away, can be a good start.
Madigan also believes governments should treat children's screen use as an important issue for their well-being.
